questions.q: A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away. What best explains this result?
options: Product differentiation gives the restaurant limited price-setting power
Free entry makes the restaurant a pure price taker
Many sellers make the restaurant demand curve perfectly elastic
The restaurant controls the entire market supply
questions.feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.

questions.q: Several new coffee shops open offering very similar drinks and service. Holding other factors constant, what is most likely to happen to the demand facing one existing shop?
options: It becomes less elastic because the market has more sellers
It becomes vertical because each shop is now smaller
It becomes perfectly inelastic because products remain differentiated
It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
questions.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to one firm’s price.

questions.q: A city has dozens of independently owned fitness studios. Each offers a somewhat different mix of classes, and new studios can enter without major legal barriers. Which model is the best starting point?
options: Monopoly
Oligopoly
Monopolistic competition
Perfect competition
questions.feedback: Many sellers, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry are the defining combination.

questions.q: A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments. Which source of differentiation is most important?
options: Identical-product pricing
Service differentiation
Resource ownership
Patent protection
questions.feedback: The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product.

questions.q: Firm A sells a differentiated snack with many close substitutes. Firm B holds an exclusive patent on a drug with no close substitute. Which comparison is most plausible?
options: Firm A faces more elastic demand than Firm B
Firm A faces less elastic demand than Firm B
Both firms face perfectly elastic demand
Both firms must face the same elasticity because each has a downward-sloping demand curve
questions.feedback: Close substitutes make buyers more responsive to Firm A’s price, while the patent shields Firm B from close substitution.

questions.q: A boutique raises its price by 4 percent and loses 7 percent of its customers, but many buyers remain because they prefer its style. What does this pattern most strongly indicate?
options: The firm is a price taker with perfectly elastic demand
The firm has monopoly power protected by an entry barrier
The market must contain only a few strategically interdependent firms
The firm has limited market power, not complete control of demand
questions.feedback: Differentiation can give a firm some control over price while close substitutes still constrain it.

questions.q: A market has many sellers and easy entry. Each seller faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its own product. Which additional fact is most consistent with monopolistic competition?
options: A single legal franchise blocks all new rivals
A few firms closely track each rival’s strategic moves
Products are differentiated but remain close substitutes
Products are identical and firms accept one market price
questions.feedback: Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.

questions.q: Food-delivery technology makes customers almost indifferent to which neighborhood a restaurant occupies. Other features are unchanged. What happens to location as a source of differentiation?
options: It turns the market into a natural monopoly
It becomes weaker because distance matters less to customers
It becomes stronger because delivery creates a new legal barrier
It guarantees each restaurant a perfectly inelastic demand curve
questions.feedback: When location matters less to buyers, location creates less product differentiation and less insulation from rivals.

questions.q: Suppose all meaningful brand, location, service, and quality differences among many sellers disappear while entry remains easy. Which competitive model does the market move toward?
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Natural monopoly
Oligopoly
questions.feedback: With many sellers, easy entry, and effectively identical products, the key remaining conditions resemble perfect competition.

questions.q: A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product. What key condition for monopolistic competition is missing?
options: A large number of sellers
Freedom of entry and exit
Independent ownership
Product differentiation
questions.feedback: Many sellers and easy entry are not enough. Monopolistic competition also requires differentiated products.

questions.q: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses its MR=MC output. At that output, price is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Raise output until price equals ATC
Exit the industry immediately because price is below ATC
Continue producing and accept an economic loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
questions.feedback: If price covers AVC, producing helps pay some fixed cost even though the firm earns an economic loss.

questions.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
options: Market supply
Marginal revenue
Average fixed cost
Long-run average cost
questions.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

questions.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Marginal revenue compared with ATC
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
questions.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

questions.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
options: Price compared with MC
MR compared with AVC
Demand compared with market supply
Price compared with ATC
questions.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

questions.q: An advertisement lists a store’s prices, hours, and warranty terms. What type of advertising is this primarily?
options: Predatory pricing
Price discrimination
Informational advertising
Persuasive advertising
questions.feedback: The message mainly reduces consumers’ information costs by providing facts.

questions.q: A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information. What type of advertising is this primarily?
options: Perfectly competitive promotion
Persuasive advertising
Informational advertising
Marginal-cost pricing
questions.feedback: The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.

questions.q: A café upgrades ingredients and service rather than cutting price. Which strategy is it using?
options: Nonprice competition through quality
A price ceiling
Perfect price discrimination
Market exit
questions.feedback: Monopolistically competitive firms often compete through quality and service as well as price.

questions.q: A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged. This is an example of:
options: Collusive pricing
A shutdown decision
Perfect competition
Nonprice competition
questions.feedback: The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price.

questions.q: A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand. If the expense is fixed, which cost curve does it directly raise?
options: Average variable cost
Marginal revenue
Average total cost
Marginal cost
questions.feedback: A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC.

questions.q: A platform charges a promotional fee on every unit a seller sells. The fee acts most like an increase in:
options: Market demand
Variable cost
Fixed cost
Consumer income
questions.feedback: A per-unit selling expense rises with output, so it behaves like a variable cost.

questions.q: A successful brand campaign causes more buyers to want the firm’s product at every price. What happens to the firm’s demand curve?
options: It shifts to the right
There is a movement down the same demand curve
It becomes the market supply curve
It shifts left because advertising raises cost
questions.feedback: A change in buyers’ willingness to purchase at each price is a demand shift, not a movement along demand.

questions.q: A loyalty campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rival brands after a price increase. The firm’s demand has become:
options: More elastic
Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic in every case
Less elastic
questions.feedback: Greater brand loyalty reduces responsiveness to the firm’s price, making demand less elastic.

questions.q: A firm develops a distinctive new feature that rivals have not yet copied. What is the most immediate competitive effect?
options: Perfectly elastic firm demand
Automatic long-run zero profit immediately
Temporary product differentiation
Guaranteed permanent monopoly
questions.feedback: A distinctive feature can temporarily strengthen differentiation until rivals respond or imitate it.

questions.q: A firm spends $20,000 on a fixed ad campaign. Demand shifts right, but MC is unchanged. Which statement is correct?
options: Profit must rise because demand shifted right
The profit-maximizing output may rise because MR changed, while the fixed ad cost also lowers profit
Output must stay unchanged because every advertising expense is fixed
MC shifts upward by exactly $20,000 at every output
questions.feedback: The demand shift can change MR and output even though the fixed selling cost itself does not shift MC.

questions.q: A comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
options: Demand becomes more elastic
Demand becomes less elastic
Demand becomes vertical
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

questions.q: A firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
options: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
ATC falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
questions.feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

questions.q: A restaurant improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
options: The cost increase alone
The old output because quality is nonprice competition
The new MR and MC curves together
The demand shift alone
questions.feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

questions.q: A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive. What becomes more plausible, other things equal?
options: A lower willingness to pay at every quantity
A larger profit-maximizing markup
A perfectly competitive price
A horizontal firm demand curve
questions.feedback: Less elastic demand can support greater price-cost markup for a firm with market power.

questions.q: Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase. Why might heavy advertising sometimes be interpreted as a quality signal?
options: A high-quality seller may expect repeat business that helps justify the advertising expense
Advertising legally guarantees the product will be high quality
Only low-quality sellers are allowed to advertise heavily
Advertising eliminates all uncertainty before purchase
questions.feedback: In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.

questions.q: Two campaigns cost the same fixed amount. Campaign A shifts demand right but leaves elasticity unchanged. Campaign B leaves demand quantity unchanged but makes demand less elastic. Why can the profit effects differ?
options: Fixed advertising cost always changes MC by the same amount
Only Campaign A can affect marginal revenue
Only Campaign B can affect the price the firm charges
The campaigns alter the firm’s revenue conditions in different ways even though both add the same fixed cost
questions.feedback: A demand shift and an elasticity change can alter MR and optimal price/output differently, while the fixed cost enters profit separately.

questions.q: A firm can spend on product quality that shifts demand right but also raises MC. Which conclusion is economically sound before seeing the magnitudes?
options: Profit must fall because marginal cost increases
Optimal output cannot change because price was not directly altered
Profit may rise or fall because both revenue and marginal cost conditions change
Profit must rise because buyers value the improvement
questions.feedback: The net effect depends on how much the improvement changes willingness to pay relative to the increase in marginal cost.

questions.q: A fixed advertising bill increases but demand does not change. Why does the MR=MC output stay the same?
options: Advertising expenses never affect profit
The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
The fixed cost lowers price by the same amount
The fixed cost raises MC at every unit
questions.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change lowers profit but does not alter the marginal decision when demand is unchanged.

questions.q: An ad tells buyers the product price and where to buy it. Why is this informational rather than persuasive?
options: It supplies facts that reduce search costs
It guarantees buyers will prefer the brand
It changes the product’s physical quality
It prevents consumers from switching brands
questions.feedback: Informational advertising communicates useful facts instead of mainly trying to reshape preferences.

questions.q: After a successful campaign, buyers purchase more at every possible price. Is this a movement along the firm’s demand curve?
options: Yes, because quantity demanded increased
Yes, because advertising changes the posted price
No, it is a leftward shift of supply
No, it is a rightward shift of demand
questions.feedback: More demanded at every price is a demand shift. A movement along demand requires a change in the firm’s own price.

questions.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Completely unwilling to buy
Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
questions.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

questions.q: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
options: A fixed monthly billboard lease
A fee charged on each unit sold
A flat annual sponsorship payment
A one-time logo redesign
questions.feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

questions.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?
options: Entry and imitation by rivals
A permanent legal ban on substitutes
Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

questions.q: Why can consumers value monopolistic competition even though firms may not produce at minimum ATC?
options: It guarantees the lowest possible price for every product
It eliminates all selling costs
It makes every firm a price taker
It offers product variety that can match different preferences
questions.feedback: Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

questions.q: In the standard long-run model, which condition signals allocative inefficiency for a monopolistically competitive firm?
options: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Economic profit equals zero
Price exceeds marginal cost
Price equals average total cost
questions.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P=MC. A positive markup means some mutually beneficial trades may not occur.

questions.q: A market has only three differentiated firms, and each changes strategy when a rival cuts price. Why may monopolistic competition be a poor model?
options: Price changes are impossible under monopolistic competition
Strategic interdependence points toward oligopoly
Differentiated products require perfect competition
Few firms automatically create a natural monopoly
questions.feedback: The monopolistic-competition model assumes many firms whose individual strategic reactions are usually not central.

questions.q: Why is a larger number of brands not automatically socially better?
options: Additional variety can create benefits but also use resources and duplicate fixed costs
Every new brand necessarily lowers marginal cost
More brands guarantee P=MC for all firms
Product variety eliminates excess capacity
questions.feedback: The welfare question compares the value of added variety with the resources used to create and sustain it.

questions.q: A policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
options: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
questions.feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

questions.q: A textbook labels a market monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
options: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
questions.feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

questions.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges P>$MC$. What does this show?
options: The firm is producing at minimum ATC
Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
The firm must be earning an accounting loss
Entry has failed to eliminate all market power
questions.feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

questions.q: Two markets have the same total production cost. Market A offers one standardized product; Market B offers several differentiated versions that consumers value. What can be said?
options: Market B may generate greater consumer benefit because variety itself can have value
Market A must be more allocatively efficient because it has fewer products
Market B must have higher deadweight loss because it has more brands
Both markets provide identical welfare because production cost is the same
questions.feedback: Equal production cost does not imply equal consumer benefit when differentiated varieties match heterogeneous preferences.

questions.q: Suppose a regulator could force every differentiated firm to price at marginal cost, but doing so would reduce firms’ ability to cover fixed product-development costs and some varieties would disappear. What is the best conclusion?
options: Marginal-cost pricing must raise welfare because P=MC is always sufficient
Variety loss is irrelevant because all firms initially earned zero economic profit
The policy must lower welfare because regulation can never improve allocation
The welfare effect depends on the gain from lower markups relative to the loss of valued variety
questions.feedback: The standard markup is inefficient, but differentiated products may create variety benefits and require fixed costs. Both sides matter.

questions.q: A monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. Does that prove the outcome is fully efficient?
options: Yes. Entry forces price to equal MC and minimum ATC
No. Zero economic profit means the firm should shut down
No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
Yes. Zero economic profit guarantees both allocative and productive efficiency
questions.feedback: Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
